hints: Focus on the little word all. Think about the thinnest, simplest blood vessel you know and what its wall looks like.
Remember which layer forms the tunica intima lining every vessel, and which layers (muscle, elastic fibres, collagen) get lost when vessels become tiny capillaries.
walkthrough:
**Spot the key word: all**

Great eye, this question is testing you on what is shared. Arteries and veins have thick walls, but capillaries and venules are very, very thin. To be in ALL vessels, a tissue must also be in a capillary.

**Recall the three tunics**

Think of a big artery. Inside to outside you have tunica intima (endothelium plus a little connective tissue), tunica media (smooth muscle plus elastic fibres), and tunica externa (collagen-rich connective tissue). Not every vessel needs all three.

**Check the capillary wall**

A capillary wall is just one cell thick to allow fast diffusion. It is only endothelium (squamous epithelium) plus its basement membrane. It has no smooth muscle to constrict, no elastic layer to stretch, and no thick collagen outer coat. So only 3, endothelial tissue, is present in every vessel.

options.A: Too generous. Capillaries do not have collagen, elastic tissue or smooth muscle, so 1, 2 and 4 cannot be in all vessels.
options.B: Close but still wrong. Collagen, elastic fibres and smooth muscle are in arteries and veins, but all three are missing from capillaries.
options.C: Endothelial tissue (3) is correct, but elastic tissue (2) is not. Capillaries have no elastic layer in their wall.
options.D: Perfect. Only the endothelial lining of the tunica intima lines every artery, arteriole, capillary, venule and vein.
